1. Core Clinical Tension: A 59-year-old male maintained on high-dose prednisone (40 mg/day) for a presumed drug eruption presents with a large, destructive 10-cm phagedenic perianal ulcer and suppurative inguinal ulcers. Upon steroid taper, disseminated erythematous papules and nodules emerge on his upper extremities. While cutaneous ulcerative lesions can be erroneously attributed to atypical erythema nodosum leprosum (type 2 lepra reaction) in an immunocompromised host, the true etiology represents a dual mycobacterial coinfection: lepromatous leprosy in the upper limbs and cutaneous perianal tuberculosis, which deteriorated despite antileprosy monotherapy.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint falls immediately after physical examination demonstrating the 10-cm phagedenic perianal ulcer, inguinal suppurative ulcers, and emerging papulonodular upper extremity lesions following steroid tapering, strictly prior to skin biopsies, histopathological staining, Lowenstein-Jensen cultures, and PCR analyses.
3. Differential Distinctions: Pyoderma gangrenosum / refractory drug eruption is excluded by infectious granulomatous histopathology and identification of mycobacteria; isolated lepromatous leprosy with necrotic type 2 lepra reaction (erythema nodosum leprosum/Lucio's phenomenon) is ruled out by lack of healing under antileprotic multidrug therapy and thalidomide, positive tuberculin skin test (20x20 mm), and positive culture of M. tuberculosis from the perianal ulcer alongside M. leprae PCR from the arm lesions.
case_prompt:
A 59-year-old male is admitted to the hospital in Botucatu, São Paulo, Brazil, complaining of a progressively worsening, painful perianal suppurative ulcer of two months' duration. For the preceding six months, he had been receiving high-dose oral corticosteroid therapy (prednisone 40 mg daily) for a presumed adverse drug reaction. Recently, as the corticosteroid dosage was gradually tapered, he noted new skin eruptions developing across his arms.

On physical examination, the patient is afebrile with stable vital signs. Anogenital examination reveals a clean, extensive 10-cm diameter phagedenic ulcer with undermined borders in the perianal region, as well as two longitudinal suppurative ulcers located in the inguino-crural folds. Cutaneous examination of the upper extremities reveals multiple disseminated erythematous papules and subcutaneous nodules across bilateral upper limbs. Regional lymph nodes are palpable in the inguinal regions. Systemic examination of the cardiovascular, respiratory, and gastrointestinal systems is otherwise within normal limits.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pyoderma Gangrenosum / Severe Cutaneous Adverse Drug Eruption
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A massive, 10-cm phagedenic perianal ulcer with purulent discharge in a patient chronically treated with prednisone for an alleged drug eruption initially suggested a neutrophilic dermatosis such as pyoderma gangrenosum or persistent severe drug vasculitis; ruled out by histopathology showing dense histiocytic granulomatous inflammation with caseous necrosis and acid-fast bacilli rather than sterile neutrophilic infiltrate.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He was under therapy with prednisone 40 mg/day for six months due to a presumed diagnosis of a drug reaction... Histopathology of the perianal ulcer revealed a dense histiocytic dermal infiltrate and a granulomatous inflammatory response with central caseous necrosis (Figure 3).

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Isolated Lepromatous Leprosy with Severe Type 2 Reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The emergence of papules and nodules containing foamy histiocytes with globi led clinicians to hypothesize that the perianal and inguinal ulcers were atypical severe necrotic manifestations of type 2 lepra reaction unmasked by steroid tapering; however, four weeks of antileprosy multidrug therapy and thalidomide resulted in worsening of the perianal ulcer, fever, and weight loss, disproving an isolated leprotic ulcer.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The histopathology of upper limbs papular and nodular lesions showed foamy macrophages with globi of bacilli, suggesting lepromatous leprosy (Figure 4). The perianal and inguinal ulcers were considered uncommon manifestations of type 2 leprosy developed when corticosteroid was gradually diminished. The patient was treated as for multibacillary leprosy with multidrug therapy and thalidomide. Four weeks later, the patient had fever, weight loss, asthenia and worsening of the perianal ulcer

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Coinfection of Lepromatous Leprosy and Cutaneous Tuberculosis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic resolution was confirmed by demonstrating two distinct mycobacterial diseases: polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from upper limb skin samples confirmed Mycobacterium leprae, while a strong tuberculin skin test (20 x 20 mm) and Lowenstein-Jensen mycobacterial culture of the perianal ulcer biopsy grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Addition of standard antituberculous therapy (isoniazid, ethambutol, rifampin) resulted in complete ulcer healing in two months, followed by curative antileprotic therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The tuberculin skin test was positive (20 x 20 mm) and culture of M. tuberculosis - using a biopsy sample from the perianal ulcer - on Lowenstein-Jensen medium was positive (Figure 6). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and DNA analysis from upper limb skin samples were positive for M. leprae (Figure 7). With the new information the patient was finally diagnosed as presenting simultaneously lepromatous leprosy - type 2 reaction - and cutaneous tuberculosis expressed by the perianal ulcer.

editor_comments: Breakpoint established before biopsy, culture, and PCR. All pathogen and disease names strictly excluded from presentation.
